original_question: Let (S^3, g) be a Riemannian 3-sphere with sectional curvature at least 1, and suppose a closed geodesic gamma is the fixed-point set of an isometric involution of (S^3, g). Must the length of gamma be at most 2*pi?
target_in_paper: Section 7, open problem titled "Involution of the 3-sphere".
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's intended problem very closely: it has the correct ambient manifold (a Riemannian 3-sphere), the correct curvature hypothesis (sectional curvature at least 1), the correct symmetry hypothesis (an isometric involution), the correct geometric object (a closed geodesic that is exactly the fixed-point set), and the correct proposed conclusion (length at most 2π).
missing_details: Make explicit that the involution is an order-two isometry iota:(S^3,g) -> (S^3,g) with iota^2 = id.
State the fixed-point hypothesis exactly as Fix(iota) = gamma, not merely that gamma is invariant under the involution.
Specify that the curvature bound is global: sec_g >= 1 for every tangent 2-plane of S^3.
Specify that the length in the conclusion is the Riemannian length with respect to g, i.e. length_g(gamma).
Do not fold in the polyhedral Alexandrov analogue mentioned in the next sentence of the paper; it is a separate follow-up question, not part of the main smooth Riemannian formulation.
refined_question: Let (S^3,g) be a Riemannian manifold diffeomorphic to the 3-sphere such that sec_g >= 1 everywhere. Suppose there exists an isometric involution iota:(S^3,g) -> (S^3,g) with iota^2 = id whose fixed-point set is a closed geodesic gamma, i.e. Fix(iota) = gamma. Must one have length_g(gamma) <= 2*pi?
justification: The draft is essentially a restatement of the exact question asked in Section 7 of the paper. The paper's wording is: suppose a closed geodesic gamma is the fixed-point set of an isometric involution of S^3; assume the sectional curvature of S^3 is at least 1; is it true that length(gamma) <= 2*pi? The nearby context in the same section adds only two remarks: first, the author asks the same question for spherical polyhedral metrics with Alexandrov curvature at least 1; second, the author notes that if one has an S^1-action instead of just an involution, then the answer is yes because the quotient is a convex disc of curvature at least 1 and gamma projects isometrically to the boundary. These are contextual remarks, not equivalent reformulations. Hence the sharp paper-faithful refinement is simply to make the metric notation and the meaning of 'isometric involution' and 'fixed-point set' completely explicit, without broadening beyond the smooth Riemannian version.
